newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche reshuffle makes sense - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche reshuffle makes sense - analysts.

text.p: Analysts on Wednesday welcomed the latest management reshuffle at Deutsche Bank AG, saying the appointment of an investment bank specialist to the top job of chief executive was a logical step given the bank's massive expansion in that area.
Deutsche, Germany's largest bank, announced management board member Rolf Bruer would replace Hilmar Kopper at the end of the next annual shareholder meeting in May 1997.
It also announced the departure of two other management board members, Ulrich Cartellieri and Ellen Schneider-Lenne, in a move which effectively reduced the management board to 10 from 12.
Breuer, 58, is among three management board members who steer Deutsche's investment banking business.

"It's only a logical step to put someone in the top job who comes from investment banking if the bank is expanding in that business," said Andreas Thielen, banking analyst at Enskilda Securities in London. "It's positive for the bank."
Share dealers also liked the news, with Deutsche's shares rising to 71.20 marks ($47.08) by 1145 GMT, up 84 pfennigs on the day.
Analysts also had praise for Hilmar Kopper, saying he had launched a much-needed reorganisation and embarked on a drive to become a globally active investment bank.
But they noted that Deutsche has in recent years also drawn a barrage of public criticism for its involvement in a series of corporate collapses.

"Kopper led the bank through an extremely difficult period and was there to accompany significant expansion moves," said Christine Winkler, banking analyst at Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel- Bank AG.

Kopper drew public outrage when he described as "peanuts" the multi-million mark losses to tradesmen arising from the 1994 collapse of the Schneider real estate group. Deutsche was Schneider's biggest creditor with an exposure of 1.2 billion marks.
"I think Kopper did a lot for the bank but got very little credit from outside," said Konrad Becker, an analyst at Merck, Finck in Frankfurt.

"He was there through a whole series of problems, the Schneider scenario, Metallgesellschaft, KHD and the rest, and also through an internal restructuring that caused great dissatisfaction in the Deutsche Bank branches. He had a very unlucky period at the bank."

Analysts said Wednesday's revamp slotted in with a management reorganisation announced in July when Deutsche split its management responsibility into four new operating areas and created an umbrella "group executive committee" to link up strategic and operational management worldwide.
The July move created four new operational divisions -- private banking, commercial and institutional banking, investment banking, and group services.

Each division has its own management team comprising senior executives responsible for day-to-day planning and at least two members of the current 12- strong management board to act as "speakers" for the division.

The "group executive committee" will comprise the management board, the divisional boards and other senior executives, including the heads of Deutsche's Asia Pacific and U.S. divisions, and is designed to ensure continuity in management decisions.
Thielen at Enskilda said Deutsche may even reduce its management board further in line with the bank's plan to focus the board's efforts on devising strategy.
